summary.text: At \(n=67\), the two distinct inputs \(147\) and \(2055\) both lie below the search bound \(2^{68}\) and have residue-sum expansions \(1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67\) and \(1+3+7+7+7+7+7+7+7+7+7=67\), respectively. Thus the relevant multiplicity is at least two, contradicting the claimed value of one.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
F(m)=\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2 m\rfloor}(m\bmod 2^k)
\]
be sequence A049802. Thus, for a positive integer \(n\), \(a(n)\) is the number of indices \(m\) for which \(F(m)=n\). In the stated finite definition, these indices are counted in the range
\[
0\le m<2^{n+1};
\]
this range is sufficient because any occurrence of the positive value \(n\) lies below that bound.

The conjecture asserts in particular that \(a(67)=1\), since \(67\) is one of
\[
1,3,5,9,15,23,35,63,65,67.
\]
We disprove this by exhibiting two distinct indices at which A049802 has value \(67\).

First take \(m=147\). Since
\[
2^7=128\le 147<256=2^8,
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 147\rfloor=7\). The required residues are
\[
\begin{array}{c|ccccccc}
k&1&2&3&4&5&6&7\\ \hline
147\bmod 2^k&1&3&3&3&19&19&19.
\end{array}
\]
Indeed, modulo \(2\) the residue is \(1\); modulo \(4,8,16\) the residue is \(3\); and
\[
147=4\cdot32+19=2\cdot64+19=1\cdot128+19,
\]
so the final three residues are all \(19\). Consequently
\[
F(147)=1+3+3+3+19+19+19=67.
\]

Next take \(m=2055\). Since
\[
2^{11}=2048\le2055<4096=2^{12},
\]
we have \(\lfloor\log_2 2055\rfloor=11\). As \(2055=2048+7\), its residues are
\[
2055\bmod2=1,
\qquad
2055\bmod4=3,
\qquad
2055\bmod8=7.
\]
For every \(k\) from \(4\) through \(11\), the number \(2^k\) divides \(2048=2^{11}\), while \(0\le7<2^k\). Hence
\[
2055\bmod 2^k=7\qquad(4\le k\le11).
\]
There are eight values of \(k\) in this last range. It follows that
\[
F(2055)=1+3+7+8\cdot7=11+56=67.
\]

The two indices are distinct. They also both lie in the finite range used to define \(a(67)\): clearly \(147<2^{68}\), and
\[
2055<4096=2^{12}<2^{68}.
\]
Therefore the set
\[
T=\left\{m:0\le m<2^{68},\ 
\sum_{k=1}^{\lfloor\log_2m\rfloor}(m\bmod2^k)=67\right\}
\]
contains both \(147\) and \(2055\). Since these are different elements, \(|T|\ge2\). By the definition of A383327, \(a(67)=|T|\), so
\[
a(67)\ge2.
\]
In particular, \(a(67)\ne1\). But \(67\) belongs to the conjecture's displayed set, so the conjecture would require \(a(67)=1\). This contradiction disproves the universal assertion.
